questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has had loose stools 5 times a day for 3 months. She often sees blood mixed with the stool, has urgency and tenesmus, and has lost 4 kg. Tender red nodules have appeared on both shins. She has no history of travel. Her temperature is 37.4°C and pulse rate 88 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic bloody diarrhoea with urgency, tenesmus, weight loss and erythema nodosum is ulcerative colitis; blood in the stool separates IBD from IBS.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Blood** with stool, **tenesmus**, weight loss and **erythema nodosum** over months.

elim: Gives non-bloody diarrhoea and bloating, not rectal bleeding with tenesmus.
Unlikely at 27, and erythema nodosum points to IBD.
Three months is too long for an untreated infection without travel.
Never causes blood in the stool or weight loss; bleeding discriminates IBD from IBS.

steps.x: **E. Ulcerative colitis.** Bloody diarrhoea + tenesmus + erythema nodosum = UC; blood rules out IBS.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man has been diagnosed with Crohn's disease after 6 months of diarrhoea, weight loss and right iliac fossa pain. He works in an office, drinks 10 units of alcohol a week and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. He took ibuprofen occasionally for back pain. He had an appendicectomy aged 12.
questions.q: Which feature of his history most increases his risk of this condition?
questions.e: Smoking is a risk factor for Crohn's disease, while it is protective in ulcerative colitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which feature of his history most increases his risk of this condition? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A young man (Crohn's peaks before **40**) who **smokes**.

elim: Not a recognised risk factor for Crohn's.
Not the key risk factor; appendicectomy is linked with lower UC risk.
NSAIDs can trigger flares but are not the main risk factor here.
Not a risk factor.

steps.x: **C. Cigarette smoking.** Smoking increases Crohn's risk but protects against UC.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman of Ashkenazi Jewish descent attends with her brother, who has just been diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. She is well, with normal bowel habit. She asks how much her own risk of developing inflammatory bowel disease is increased because of her brother's diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the best estimate of the increase in her risk?
questions.e: A first-degree relative with UC gives a seven-fold increase in the risk of IBD; Jewish and white European descent also increase risk.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the best estimate of the increase in her risk? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **first-degree relative** with UC, in an at-risk ethnic group.

elim: Far too high; IBD is polygenic, not single-gene.
Family history is one of the strongest risk factors.
Too high.
Underestimates the risk.

steps.x: **C. Seven-fold.** First-degree relative with UC = seven-fold increased IBD risk.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy has had colicky abdominal pain and non-bloody diarrhoea for 5 months. He has lost 8 kg and has aphthous mouth ulcers. There is a tender mass in the right iliac fossa (see item resources). His haemoglobin is 104 g/L and faecal calprotectin is 780 µg/g.

visual.title: Where the mass is
visual.caption: Tender mass in the right iliac fossa.

questions.q: Which part of the bowel is most likely to be affected?
questions.e: Crohn's disease most commonly affects the terminal ileum, giving right iliac fossa pain and a mass, with anaemia and weight loss.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which part of the bowel is most likely to be affected? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Non-bloody diarrhoea, mouth ulcers, weight loss and an **RIF mass** = Crohn's.

elim: Crohn's can affect it but rarely; the right iliac fossa mass points to the ileum.
The site where UC always starts; Crohn's often spares it.
Would give left iliac fossa signs.
Not the commonest site and not in the right iliac fossa.

steps.x: **D. Terminal ileum.** Crohn's: commonest site is the terminal ileum (RIF mass).

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has passed small amounts of blood and mucus several times a day for 6 weeks, with tenesmus. His stools are otherwise formed. Rigid sigmoidoscopy shows continuous granular, inflamed mucosa from the anal verge to 12 cm, with normal mucosa above. Stool cultures are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bloody mucoid discharge with tenesmus and continuous inflammation limited to the rectum is ulcerative proctitis; UC always starts at the rectum.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: continuous granular, inflamed mucosa from the anal verge
steps.x: Continuous inflammation **starting at the rectum** and stopping at 12 cm, with **tenesmus and mucus**.

elim: Causes pain on defaecation with bright red blood, not continuous inflamed mucosa.
Gives patchy skip lesions and usually spares the rectum.
Do not cause mucosal inflammation or tenesmus.
Gives a mass or ulcer, not continuous granular inflammation.

steps.x: **E. Ulcerative proctitis.** Proctitis: bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus, mucus; UC always involves the rectum.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has had bloody diarrhoea 4 times a day for 2 months. Faecal calprotectin is 540 µg/g and stool cultures are negative. Her consultant suspects extensive ulcerative colitis and arranges colonoscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on colonoscopy?
o: Cobblestone mucosa of the terminal ileum
Continuous inflammation from the rectum to the mid-transverse colon
Deep fissuring ulcers with rectal sparing
Multiple discrete inflamed areas with normal mucosa between
questions.e: UC causes continuous, symmetrical mucosal inflammation from the anal verge proximally, reaching the mid-transverse colon in extensive disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on colonoscopy? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
UC: **continuous** mucosal disease, **from the rectum** upward.

elim: Crohn's disease.
Crohn's colitis.
Skip lesions, typical of Crohn's.
Microscopic colitis, which gives watery non-bloody diarrhoea.

steps.x: **B. Continuous inflammation from the rectum to the mid-transverse colon.** UC = continuous from the rectum; Crohn's = skip lesions and cobblestones.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man with ulcerative colitis has had 7 bloody stools a day for 5 days. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. His abdomen is soft and mildly tender.
questions.q: Which finding makes this a severe flare by Truelove and Witts' criteria?
questions.e: Severe UC is 6 or more bloody stools a day plus one of Hb below 105 g/L, temperature above 37.8°C, pulse above 90 bpm or ESR above 30 mm/hour.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which finding makes this a severe flare by Truelove and Witts' criteria? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
He has **≥6 bloody stools**; now look for the one systemic feature over its cut-off.

elim: Not one of the Truelove and Witts' criteria.
Below the threshold of 30 mm/hour.
Below the threshold of 90 bpm.
Below the threshold of 37.8°C.

steps.x: **C. Haemoglobin 98 g/L.** Truelove and Witts': ≥6 bloody stools + Hb <105, T >37.8, HR >90 or ESR >30.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis has had 2 months of painless jaundice, itching and 7 kg weight loss. His ALP is 640 IU/L and ALT 88 IU/L. CA 19-9 is markedly raised. MRCP shows a hilar stricture with upstream bile duct dilatation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: PSC in UC predisposes to cholangiocarcinoma, suggested by painless jaundice, weight loss, a dominant stricture and a raised CA 19-9.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
UC with PSC, now weight loss and a **stricture** with raised **CA 19-9**.

elim: Gallstones give pain and do not raise CA 19-9 this much.
Arises in cirrhosis and raises alpha-fetoprotein.
Gives epigastric pain and raised amylase.
Affects small intrahepatic ducts in middle-aged women; no stricture or weight loss.

steps.x: **A. Cholangiocarcinoma.** UC complications: PSC and cholangiocarcinoma (CA 19-9).

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum has fatigue and tingling in both feet. She had an ileal resection 3 years ago. Her haemoglobin is 96 g/L with an MCV of 112 fL. Folate is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
questions.e: B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum, so ileal Crohn's or resection causes malabsorption and B12 deficiency with macrocytosis and neuropathy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Macrocytic** anaemia with **neuropathy** after **terminal ileal** disease and resection.

elim: Usually normocytic, and does not cause neuropathy.
Folate is normal.
Gives a microcytic anaemia.
Gives microcytosis and no neuropathy.

steps.x: **E. Vitamin B12 deficiency.** Terminal ileal Crohn's: B12 malabsorption.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man with long-standing Crohn's disease has severe colicky pain radiating from his left loin to his groin, with vomiting. He is writhing on the trolley. Urine dipstick shows blood. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. His abdomen is soft.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Renal stones are an extra-intestinal feature of Crohn's disease; loin-to-groin colic with haematuria in a restless patient is a renal stone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Loin-to-groin** colic, restless, **haematuria**.

elim: Gives pneumaturia and recurrent UTIs, not loin-to-groin colic.
He would have peritonism and lie still.
Gives distension and central colic, not loin-to-groin pain.
A complication of colitis with distension and systemic toxicity.

steps.x: **C. Renal calculus.** Crohn's raises renal stone risk (oxalate absorption from fat malabsorption).

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with ulcerative colitis has a painful red right eye with blurred vision for 2 days. Bright light makes the pain worse. The redness is most marked around the iris and the pupil is small. There is no discharge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Painful red eye with photophobia, circumcorneal redness and a small pupil is anterior uveitis, an extra-intestinal manifestation of IBD.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Bright light makes the pain worse
steps.x: **Photophobia**, ciliary flush and a **small pupil**.

elim: Gives a fixed mid-dilated pupil, not a small pupil, and is uncommon at 31.
Gives discharge with normal vision.
Also linked to IBD, but is mildly uncomfortable with no photophobia or visual loss.
Painless red patch.

steps.x: **B. Anterior uveitis.** IBD eye: uveitis (painful, photophobia), episcleritis (mild), scleritis.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man with ulcerative colitis has a painful ulcer on his left shin that began as a small pustule after he knocked his leg 3 weeks ago. It has enlarged rapidly to 5 cm, with a purple, undermined edge. Wound swabs grow no pathogens. He is having a flare of his colitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge after minor trauma (pathergy) in IBD is pyoderma gangrenosum.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A rapidly growing **undermined** ulcer starting as a **pustule** in IBD.

elim: Small punched-out ulcers on the foot in older vascular patients.
Spreading erythema, not a necrotic ulcer with an undermined edge.
Tender red nodules that do not ulcerate.
Shallow, painless ulcer above the medial malleolus.

steps.x: **D. Pyoderma gangrenosum.** IBD skin: erythema nodosum (nodules) and pyoderma gangrenosum (ulcer).

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with Crohn's disease has had low back pain and buttock pain for 6 months. It is worst in the morning, with stiffness lasting an hour, and improves with exercise. He wakes in the second half of the night with pain. His Crohn's is in remission. Lumbar flexion is reduced.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness, better with exercise, night pain) in IBD is ankylosing spondylitis or sacroiliitis, an extra-intestinal manifestation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: wakes in the second half of the night
steps.x: **Inflammatory** back pain: morning stiffness, better with **exercise**.

elim: Mechanical pain made worse by activity, often with sciatica.
Worse with activity and better with rest.
Sudden pain, usually in older people or after steroids.
Unlikely at 28, with constant pain and red flags.

steps.x: **A. Ankylosing spondylitis.** IBD joints: ankylosing spondylitis, sacroiliitis, seronegative small-joint arthritis.

questions.stem: A 21 year old man has had painful defaecation and a discharging opening beside his anus for 2 months. He also has 4 months of non-bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and 6 kg weight loss. Examination shows large anal skin tags, a posterior fissure and an external fistula opening.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Perianal disease (skin tags, fissures, fistulae) with non-bloody diarrhoea and weight loss is characteristic of Crohn's disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Perianal disease** (skin tags, fissure, fistula) plus diarrhoea and weight loss.

elim: Does not cause perianal disease.
Do not cause fistulae or weight loss.
Causes no weight loss or perianal disease.
Mucosal disease that rarely causes fistulae.

steps.x: **B. Crohn's disease.** Perianal fistulae and skin tags = Crohn's.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has had non-bloody diarrhoea and 5 kg weight loss for 3 months. Colonoscopy shows several separate areas of deep ulceration in the caecum and ascending colon, with normal mucosa between them, and a cobblestone appearance of the terminal ileum. Biopsies show no malignancy and no caseation. She has never travelled.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Skip lesions with cobblestoning of the terminal ileum is Crohn's disease; there is a smaller second age peak in older patients.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Skip lesions** and **cobblestones**, even at 68.

elim: Biopsies show no malignancy.
Causes caseating granulomas and usually follows exposure in endemic areas.
Acute, painful and bloody, not chronic skip lesions.
Continuous from the rectum; never causes skip lesions or ileal cobblestoning.

steps.x: **B. Crohn's disease.** Crohn's has a second, smaller peak in older people; skip lesions are the clue.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with acute severe ulcerative colitis has had IV hydrocortisone for 4 days. She now has fewer stools but increasing abdominal pain and distension. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 88/52 mmHg, and she is drowsy. Her abdomen is markedly tender. Abdominal X-ray shows the transverse colon is 8 cm in diameter.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Colon over 6 cm with fever over 38°C, pulse over 120 bpm, plus hypotension or altered consciousness in UC not responding to IV steroids is toxic megacolon.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Colon **>6 cm**, **fever >38**, **HR >120**, plus **hypotension and drowsiness**.

elim: Steroids rarely cause it; colonic dilatation is not a feature.
Unlikely at 34 during a colitis flare.
Pseudo-obstruction without colitis or toxicity.
Gives a coffee-bean sigmoid loop, not transverse dilatation in fulminant colitis.

steps.x: **E. Toxic megacolon.** Toxic megacolon: dilatation >6 cm + 3 systemic signs + 1 of shock, confusion, dehydration or electrolytes.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman has had diarrhoea, abdominal pain and 5 kg weight loss for 4 months. She has mouth ulcers. Faecal calprotectin is 650 µg/g. Stool cultures are negative. Coeliac serology is negative. Her temperature is 37.2°C and pulse rate 84 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Colonoscopy with biopsy (including the terminal ileum) is the gold standard for diagnosing IBD.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Raised calprotectin with features of **Crohn's**: now confirm it.

elim: Used for small bowel disease not reached by colonoscopy; risk of retention in strictures.
Shows complications, not mucosal histology.
Stages extent of Crohn's once diagnosed, not the gold standard.
Already raised; it cannot confirm the diagnosis.

steps.x: **C. Ileocolonoscopy with biopsy.** Gold standard for IBD: colonoscopy with biopsy.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man presents with 10 bloody stools a day for 6 days. He has no previous bowel history. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Haemoglobin is 101 g/L and CRP 96 mg/L. Abdominal X-ray shows no colonic dilatation. Stool cultures are pending.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: In acute severe colitis, unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy is used instead of full colonoscopy because of the perforation risk.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
This is a **severe** colitis flare (Truelove and Witts'), so full colonoscopy is risky.

elim: Risks perforation and toxic dilatation in acute colitis.
Needs bowel preparation and insufflation; not for acute severe colitis.
The gold standard normally, but too risky for perforation in a severe flare.
Stages small bowel Crohn's; not for acute colitis.

steps.x: **C. Flexible sigmoidoscopy without bowel preparation.** Severe flare: unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy, not colonoscopy.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has had bloody diarrhoea and urgency for 3 months. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from the rectum to the splenic flexure. Biopsies are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on biopsy?
o: Crypt abscesses with goblet cell depletion
Increased goblet cells with submucosal fibrosis
questions.e: UC biopsy shows surface mucosal inflammation, crypt abscesses, loss of goblet cells (mucin depletion) and basal plasmacytosis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on biopsy? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Continuous colitis from the rectum = **UC**, which is mucosal disease.

elim: Features of Crohn's disease.
Coeliac disease of the small bowel.
Crohn's disease.
Microscopic (collagenous) colitis.

steps.x: **A. Crypt abscesses with goblet cell depletion.** UC histology: crypt abscesses, goblet cell loss; Crohn's: transmural, non-caseating granulomas.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss. Colonoscopy shows patchy deep ulcers in the terminal ileum and right colon with normal intervening mucosa. Biopsies are taken from the ulcer edges.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on histology?
o: Crypt abscesses confined to the mucosa
Diffuse mucosal atrophy with goblet cell loss
questions.e: Crohn's disease shows transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas (a Th1 response), submucosal fibrosis and preserved or increased goblet cells.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on histology? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Skip lesions in the terminal ileum = **Crohn's**.

elim: Suggest tuberculosis.
Typical of UC.
Typical of UC.
C. difficile colitis.

steps.x: **D. Non-caseating granulomas with transmural inflammation.** Crohn's histology: transmural, non-caseating granulomas.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has had loose stools 3 to 4 times a day with crampy lower abdominal pain for 3 months. He has not seen any blood. His weight is stable. Examination is normal. Full blood count, CRP and coeliac serology are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Faecal calprotectin helps distinguish IBD from IBS in young adults with chronic diarrhoea; a raised result leads to colonoscopy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Young man with chronic diarrhoea, **no blood**, no weight loss: is it IBD or IBS?

elim: Not first line when the picture may be IBS; calprotectin decides who needs it.
Not indicated with normal examination and bloods.
Invasive, not the first step.
For staging established Crohn's.

steps.x: **C. Faecal calprotectin.** IBD or IBS? Faecal calprotectin first.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with known ulcerative colitis has a flare with 5 bloody stools a day for a week. She feels tired. Her temperature is 37.5°C and pulse rate 88 bpm. Blood tests are sent.
questions.q: Which set of blood results is most likely?
o: Low haemoglobin, normal CRP and normal ESR
Low haemoglobin, raised CRP and raised ESR
Normal haemoglobin, low CRP and low ESR
Raised haemoglobin, raised CRP and normal ESR
Raised platelets, low CRP and low ESR
questions.e: Active IBD raises CRP and ESR, and anaemia is common from blood loss and chronic inflammation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which set of blood results is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Active** colitis with blood loss.

elim: Active inflammation usually raises the inflammatory markers.
CRP and ESR are not lowered in a flare.
Bleeding and chronic inflammation lower haemoglobin.
A flare raises, not lowers, CRP and ESR.

steps.x: **B. Low haemoglobin, raised CRP and raised ESR.** Bloods in active IBD: raised CRP and ESR, anaemia.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man with ulcerative colitis is on day 3 of IV hydrocortisone. His abdomen has become distended and very tender. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the abdominal X-ray?
o: Coffee-bean loop arising from the pelvis
Dilated small bowel loops with valvulae conniventes
Transverse colon dilated to more than 6 cm
questions.e: Toxic megacolon shows a grossly dilated colon over 6 cm on abdominal X-ray, often the transverse colon.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on the abdominal X-ray? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fulminant colitis with distension and toxicity: suspect **toxic megacolon**.

elim: Sigmoid volvulus.
Small bowel obstruction.
Gallstone ileus or previous sphincterotomy.
Unlikely with this distension and toxicity.

steps.x: **E. Transverse colon dilated to more than 6 cm.** Toxic megacolon on AXR: colon >6 cm.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with Crohn's disease has had worsening throbbing pain beside her anus for 4 days, making sitting difficult. Her temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. There is a tender, indurated area lateral to the anus. A complex fistula is suspected.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Suspected perianal abscess or complex fistula in Crohn's needs urgent MRI pelvis to map collections and tracts.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: indurated area lateral to the anus
steps.x: Painful, indurated perianal area with fever in **Crohn's** = possible **abscess**.

elim: Does not show perianal abscesses.
Images the small bowel lumen, not perianal tracts.
Assesses mucosa, not perianal collections.
Less good than MRI for fistula anatomy.

steps.x: **E. Urgent MRI pelvis.** Perianal Crohn's abscess or fistula: urgent MRI pelvis.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has newly diagnosed Crohn's disease confirmed on colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsies. His gastroenterologist wants to know how much of his small bowel is involved and whether there are strictures before planning treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: MRI small bowel is the best way to evaluate the stage and extent of Crohn's disease, without radiation.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: how much of his small bowel is involved
steps.x: Staging the **extent** of small bowel Crohn's.

elim: Operator dependent and less complete than MRI.
Cannot assess extent of small bowel disease.
Useful in emergencies but involves repeated radiation in young people.
Only reaches the duodenum.

steps.x: **D. MRI small bowel.** Extent of Crohn's: MRI small bowel.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with Crohn's disease has not responded to azathioprine and methotrexate. Her gastroenterologist plans to start infliximab. She was born in India and moved to the UK aged 14. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most important investigation before starting treatment?
questions.e: Anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab can reactivate tuberculosis, so a chest X-ray is done first to exclude prior or active TB.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most important investigation before starting treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Starting **anti-TNF** in someone from a TB-endemic area.

elim: Relevant to long-term steroids, not anti-TNF safety.
Not routine before anti-TNF therapy.
Monitors activity but does not affect safety.
Checked before azathioprine, not anti-TNF.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray.** Before infliximab: chest X-ray for TB (plus hepatitis B, C and HIV screen).

questions.stem: A 41 year old man with newly diagnosed moderate ulcerative colitis is to start oral prednisolone and is likely to need further immunosuppression later. He has no other medical history. His chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation before immunosuppression?
o: Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology
questions.e: Before steroids, biologics or other immunosuppressants, patients are screened for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV, which can flare when immunity is suppressed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate additional investigation before immunosuppression? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Immunosuppression** is planned; TB has been looked at. What else can reactivate?

elim: Not needed before immunosuppression.
Coeliac screening, not a safety test.
Not routine before steroids.
No relevance to immunosuppression.

steps.x: **C. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology.** Before immunosuppression: screen for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with ulcerative colitis has fatigue and itching. He is not jaundiced. His ALP is 420 IU/L, ALT 52 IU/L and bilirubin 18 µmol/L. Abdominal ultrasound shows no gallstones and no dilated ducts.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: In UC, a disproportionately raised ALP suggests primary sclerosing cholangitis, which is diagnosed on MRCP (beading of the bile ducts).

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**ALP raised far more than ALT** in UC = cholestasis: think **PSC**.

elim: For primary biliary cholangitis, which is not associated with UC.
Invasive with a risk of pancreatitis; reserved for treatment.
Not needed when MRCP shows typical changes.
A tumour marker for cholangiocarcinoma, not a diagnostic test for PSC.

steps.x: **D. MRCP.** PSC in UC: ALP >> ALT, diagnosed on MRCP.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with mild left-sided ulcerative colitis started rectal mesalazine 4 weeks ago. She still opens her bowels 4 times a day with a little blood. She is well. Her temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop rectal mesalazine and start oral prednisolone
questions.e: Per NICE guidance, mild to moderate UC is induced with topical mesalazine; if that is not enough, oral mesalazine is added and both are continued.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: 4 times a day with a little blood
steps.x: Mild-moderate UC not settling on **topical** 5-ASA alone.

elim: For maintenance after frequent relapses, not induction.
For severe UC only.
A rescue option after steroids fail.
Topical treatment is continued; steroids come only if 5-ASA fails.

steps.x: **B. Add oral mesalazine.** UC induction: topical mesalazine, then add oral 5-ASA.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man with ulcerative colitis has 5 bloody stools a day despite 4 weeks of rectal mesalazine and high-dose oral mesalazine. He is well in himself. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, and haemoglobin 128 g/L.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Moderate UC failing topical and oral aminosalicylates is treated by adding an oral corticosteroid such as prednisolone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: despite 4 weeks of rectal mesalazine and high-dose oral mesalazine
